messages.subject: Usage of occu() vs. colext()
parts:
Hi everyone,

I am currently working on my master thesis and I want to find out habitat preferences of my study species. I therefor collected presence absence data of the species with wildlife cameras (20 cameras, 2 years, same location and dates) and footprint tunnels (100 tunnels, 1 year, 14 repetitions). Same parameters were collected on every camera (both years) and footprint location. In addition, some more habitat parameters were collected for the tunnels and in the second year of the cameras. The second year of the cameras is the same time period as the data collection of the tunnels.

I now have questions about the usage of the functions colext() and occu().

First of all, I am analysing both datasets separately, because I assume detection probability to be different among both methods, is that correct?

Cameras:

1.       I am using function colext() for multi-season occupancy models because I have data of two years. But two seasons are not enough to calculate colonisation and extinction, as far as I understood. Would it therefor make more sense to use as single season occupancy model (function occu())? If so, how do I deal with different habitat parameters and different values for parameters collected in both years? I was using colext() to account for changes between the years.

2.       When using colext() for my camera data I have two primary periods and 146 secondary periods (number of days when cameras where operating). That seems quite a lot to me for the secondary periods. Does it make the model worse if the number of primary periods is that high?

Tunnels:

I tried both functions for tunnel data (even though I only have one year) and for colext I created five primary periods (one for every month). For both functions I get significant results for some covariates, but they do differ between the functions. With colext function I get lower AICs than with occu function. Should I therefor prefer the multi-season framework for the tunnels?

Depending on your opinion I am also thinking on creating more primary periods for cameras (1 month = 1 primary period), as I also did for tunnels. Or would it be better to do the opposite and run single season models which include both years?

I am very happy for every suggestions! Thanks a lot in advance!

Hanna

messages.author: e5388b3d81309a1f
messages.subject: Re: Usage of occu() vs. colext()
parts:
One addition: 
I was reading this in the unmarked group:  you cannot fit yearly site-covariates in a study with only 2 primarly occasions, since yearly site-covariates are used to explain variation in the dynamic rate params (colonisation, extinction). But with only two primary occasions, you only have a single colonisation and a single extinction parameter, hence, you can only try to explain spatial, but not spatio-temporal variation in them. That’s done by fitting site covariates.

This would be the case for me as well. But so far, I do not understand how to use my covariates appropriate. For example I have shrub cover for both years. If I do not use it as a yearly site-covariate, but as two site covariates (shrub2021 and shrub2022) the values of each site covariate will be applied to my whole dataset, right? So shrub2021 will be applied to the detection data of year 2021 and 2022 even though shrub2021 only describes the shrub cover in year 2021. 
How can I refer the covariates to the primary periods (year 2021 and 2022) without using yearly site-covariates or using the average? Or is it just not possible because at least 3 primary periods are needed? 

Best regards
Hanna

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: AW: [unmarked] Re: Usage of occu() vs. colext()
parts:
Dear Hanna,

 

couple of comments:

  • Normally I’d analyse both data sets together and simply treat the detection method as a covariate for detection. Although: this assumes that both methods sample space in the same way, e.g., it would not be good if you have one method in the forest and the other in the open.
  • When using colext, you can estimate one occupancy parameter for the start, i.e. for year 1, and then one set of colonization and extinction params. You have only a single annual interval, and these params governing the dynamics are defined per interval, not per year. In other words, you then have only spatial variation in col and ext, but not temporal variation
  • Thus, since there is only a single col and ext parameter, you cannot have yearly site covariates on them, but only site covariates
  • If you want to use site covariates to explain spatial variation in col and ext, it would probably make most sense to use covariates that are measured during the first year or else during the annual interval, but not during the second year
  • For the cameras, I’d probably aggregate daily data to weekly data. This makes the data set more manageable and will reduce the temporal autocorrelation that might otherwise exist (and which cannot be taken into account in colext).
  • You can’t compare the AIC between occu() and colext() since the likelihood differs
  • Overall, I have to say, that if you’re not particularly interested in explaining the change (and you can do it with one of the data sets only anyway), I’d probably use occu() on a stacked data analysis.

 

Best regards  --- Marc

 

PS: What’s the animal ?

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: AW: [unmarked] Re: Usage of occu() vs. colext()
parts:
Dear Hanna,

 

nice critters, these dormice. Couple comments back:

  • Doing separate and joint analyses seems sensible. Normally, one would hope that inferences should not change drastically when going from separate to joint. If they do, then this might indicate some problems, e.g., that two methods detect different parts of a population etc.
  • I don’t understand your line starting with “About using colext”.
  • Then, it is NOT the case that with occu() you can only model static populations ! Rather, with occu() in your case I would add Year as a factor and hence stratify the analyses by year. That way, you estimate different parameters in each year. Comparison of such a model with year-specific parameters to a simpler model where you assume parameters are constant across years provides a test of change at the level of occupancy and/or detection.

 

Best regards  --- Marc

parts:
Dear Hanna,

you have (at least) two ways of viewing your data: either via a static model which has one parameter of occupancy in year 1 and another in year 2. You can fit such a model using occu() by treating Year as a factor. Or, as a dynamic model where you have one occupancy parameter in year 1 and then an extinction (eps) and colonization (gamma) parameter for the transition from year 1 to year 2. This model you can fit with colext(). In a sense, the pair of (eps, gamma) in the dynamic model replaces the occupancy parameter in the second year from the first model (the one you fit with with occu()).

So, I suggest to think very clearly about the chronology of events in the occupancy process, along with the possible covariates. In the model you can fit with occu(), you have two parameters at time points 1 and 2. In the model that you fit with colext(), you have one parameter at time 1 and two more that belong somewhere to time 1.5. So, (unless near- or totally constant over time) a covariate that you measure in year 2 is unlikely to be a sensible predictor for spatial variation in the dynamics parameters (eps, gamma), since at the time when you measure this covariate, the state transition has already taken place.

Perhaps it helps if you make some pictures of the temporal dynamics of the processes in question ?

Best regards  -- Marc

nice critters, these dormice. Couple comments back:

  • Doing separate and joint analyses seems sensible. Normally, one would hope that inferences should not change drastically when going from separate to joint. If they do, then this might indicate some problems, e.g., that two methods detect different parts of a population etc.
  • I don’t understand your line starting with “About using colext”.
  • Then, it is NOT the case that with occu() you can only model static populations ! Rather, with occu() in your case I would add Year as a factor and hence stratify the analyses by year. That way, you estimate different parameters in each year. Comparison of such a model with year-specific parameters to a simpler model where you assume parameters are constant across years provides a test of change at the level of occupancy and/or detection.

Dear Hanna,

 

couple of comments:

  • Normally I’d analyse both data sets together and simply treat the detection method as a covariate for detection. Although: this assumes that both methods sample space in the same way, e.g., it would not be good if you have one method in the forest and the other in the open.
  • When using colext, you can estimate one occupancy parameter for the start, i.e. for year 1, and then one set of colonization and extinction params. You have only a single annual interval, and these params governing the dynamics are defined per interval, not per year. In other words, you then have only spatial variation in col and ext, but not temporal variation
  • Thus, since there is only a single col and ext parameter, you cannot have yearly site covariates on them, but only site covariates
  • If you want to use site covariates to explain spatial variation in col and ext, it would probably make most sense to use covariates that are measured during the first year or else during the annual interval, but not during the second year
  • For the cameras, I’d probably aggregate daily data to weekly data. This makes the data set more manageable and will reduce the temporal autocorrelation that might otherwise exist (and which cannot be taken into account in colext).
  • You can’t compare the AIC between occu() and colext() since the likelihood differs
  • Overall, I have to say, that if you’re not particularly interested in explaining the change (and you can do it with one of the data sets only anyway), I’d probably use occu() on a stacked data analysis.

 

Best regards  --- Marc
